questions.passage: In 2019, archaeologist Elena Marquez used ground-penetrating radar to examine parts of Pompeii that had not been excavated. At the University of Naples Federico II, her team compared the radar images with maps of nearby Roman houses. The images revealed walls and courtyards beneath the surface, allowing the researchers to identify the layout of several buried structures without digging them up. The project showed that radar can help archaeologists study Pompeii while limiting physical disturbance to the site.
questions.question: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.A: Ground-penetrating radar can help archaeologists investigate Pompeii while reducing the need for excavation.
choices.B: Roman houses in Pompeii were generally larger than archaeologists had previously believed.
choices.C: Elena Marquez's team created the first complete map of Pompeii's buried structures.
choices.D: The University of Naples Federico II specializes in technologies for studying Roman architecture.

questions.explanation: The passage explains that Marquez's team used radar to identify buried structures without excavating them and concludes that the method can reduce physical disturbance. The other choices either focus on unsupported details or make claims the passage does not establish.

questions.passage: When archaeologist Elena Marquez and colleagues at the University of Naples Federico II surveyed an unexcavated section of Pompeii in 2019, they did not begin by removing soil. Instead, they used ground-penetrating radar and compared its readings with maps of nearby Roman houses. The resulting images suggested the presence of walls, courtyards, and other structural features below the surface. Because these features could be mapped without exposing them, the team could reconstruct portions of the area's layout while leaving the archaeological deposits largely undisturbed. The work therefore demonstrated that remote sensing can provide useful information about Pompeii while avoiding some of the physical disruption associated with conventional excavation.
questions.question: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.A: Maps of Roman houses are more useful than radar images for reconstructing Pompeii's buried structures.
choices.B: Ground-penetrating radar can reveal information about buried structures at Pompeii while allowing archaeologists to limit physical disturbance.
choices.C: Marquez's team's findings suggest that remote sensing can substantially reduce the need for conventional excavation at Pompeii.
choices.D: The structural features discovered by Elena Marquez's team were previously unknown to archaeologists.

questions.explanation: The passage connects the radar readings and existing maps to the team's ability to reconstruct buried structures without exposing them. Its central point is therefore that remote sensing can provide archaeological information while limiting physical disturbance. A and D misrepresent supporting details, while C extends the passage's claim beyond what it establishes.

questions.passage: At Pompeii, archaeologists face a practical dilemma when studying structures still hidden beneath volcanic deposits: excavation can reveal architectural details, but exposing deposits also alters the archaeological record. In 2019, Elena Marquez and colleagues at the University of Naples Federico II used ground-penetrating radar to examine an unexcavated area. The survey produced patterns indicating walls, courtyards, and other features, but individual signals required interpretation and did not reveal the same material information as excavation. In several selected areas, later excavation exposed structures that corresponded to patterns identified in the radar images, while other signals proved less conclusive. In one excavated section, the wall alignments matched several radar anomalies, whereas a nearby signal did not correspond to a clearly identifiable structure.
questions.question: Which choice best states the central idea of the passage?

choices.A: Ground-penetrating radar provides archaeologists with more detailed information than conventional excavation does.
choices.B: Elena Marquez's survey established that the buried architecture of Pompeii can be completely reconstructed without excavation.
choices.C: Although radar cannot provide all the information that excavation can, it can reveal useful evidence about buried structures before excavation and thereby limit unnecessary physical disturbance.
choices.D: The main purpose of comparing radar images with maps of Roman houses is to determine which areas of Pompeii should eventually be excavated.

questions.explanation: The passage shows both the usefulness and the limitation of radar: it can identify structural evidence before deposits are disturbed, and some of those interpretations are later supported by excavation, but it cannot answer every archaeological question by itself. Choice C captures that full relationship. A reverses the limitation, B overstates what the survey established, and D narrows the passage to one possible use of the method.

questions.passage: Since Eurasian beavers (*Castor fiber*) were reintroduced to Scotland, researchers have studied how their dams affect the movement of water. At Knapdale Forest, biologists observed that dams slowed water and temporarily stored some of it in ponds. During heavy rainfall, this storage delayed part of the runoff from reaching downstream channels all at once. As a result, water reached some downstream areas more gradually than it otherwise would have.
questions.question: Which inference is best supported by the passage?

choices.A: Beaver dams prevent heavy rainfall from entering Scottish streams.
choices.B: Knapdale Forest receives less rainfall than areas without beaver dams.
choices.C: Beaver dams permanently remove some stormwater from downstream channels.
choices.D: Beaver dams may reduce the intensity of some downstream flooding by delaying runoff.

questions.explanation: The passage explains that beaver dams slow water and temporarily store some runoff, causing it to reach downstream channels more gradually. It is therefore reasonable to infer that the dams may reduce the intensity of some downstream flooding. A, B, and C make claims that the passage does not support.

questions.passage: The return of Eurasian beavers (*Castor fiber*) to Scotland has given researchers an opportunity to examine how dam building affects water movement. At Knapdale Forest, monitoring showed that beaver structures could increase temporary water storage and delay the arrival of peak flows downstream. This effect would not make flooding impossible: stored water eventually leaves the ponds, and the amount of delay can vary with local conditions. Nevertheless, when runoff is slowed before reaching downstream channels, some of the water may arrive over a longer period rather than in a concentrated surge.
questions.question: Which inference is best supported by the passage?

choices.A: Beaver colonies may lessen the severity of some downstream floods by spreading the arrival of runoff over time.
choices.B: Beaver dams are most useful for preventing flooding when rainfall is relatively light.
choices.C: The presence of beavers guarantees that downstream flooding will remain minor.
choices.D: The Knapdale monitoring showed that beaver dams permanently retain stormwater.

questions.explanation: The passage states that beaver structures can temporarily store water and delay peak flows. Because some runoff may therefore reach downstream channels over a longer period instead of as a concentrated surge, it can be inferred that beaver colonies may lessen the severity of some floods. B, C, and D either add unsupported claims or contradict the passage's description of temporary storage.

questions.passage: The reintroduction of Eurasian beavers (*Castor fiber*) to Scotland has provided researchers with a way to examine how habitat modification can alter the timing of water movement. At Knapdale Forest, monitoring found that beaver structures could increase temporary storage and delay peak flows in some downstream streams. That observation does not mean that an individual dam can prevent flooding, since water stored in a pond eventually continues downstream and the amount of storage can change during a storm. The hydrological effect also depends on where dams occur within a drainage network. A structure located farther upstream, for example, can affect when part of its stored water reaches downstream channels, while a separate structure elsewhere in the same network can alter the timing of another portion of the runoff. Taken together, these observations indicate that the effect of beaver activity should be considered not only in terms of how much water a single pond can hold, but also in terms of how multiple temporary delays change the timing of runoff across a larger drainage system.
questions.question: Which inference is best supported by the passage?

choices.A: Because individual ponds eventually release stored water, beaver dams have little influence on downstream flood flows.
choices.B: Beaver dams can prevent major floods only when each pond remains below capacity throughout a storm.
choices.C: Several beaver dams distributed through a drainage network may moderate some downstream flooding by collectively delaying runoff, even though no individual dam guarantees flood prevention.
choices.D: The Knapdale study demonstrated that beaver structures are more effective than engineered flood-control systems.

questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes between the limited effect of an individual dam and the combined effect of temporary delays at different points in a drainage network. Because multiple structures can alter when different portions of runoff reach downstream channels, their cumulative effect may moderate some downstream flooding even though none can guarantee that flooding will be prevented. A treats the eventual release of stored water as evidence that dams have little effect, ignoring the importance of delayed timing. B incorrectly assumes that permanent or uninterrupted storage is necessary. D introduces a comparison with engineered flood-control systems that the passage never makes.

questions.passage: Mangrove forests can reduce the force of coastal storms. In Florida’s Everglades, the red mangrove (*Rhizophora mangle*) forms dense networks of trunks and roots that slow moving water. Field measurements from the Ten Thousand Islands have shown that water loses energy as it passes through wider mangrove stands. However, a narrow or damaged stand provides less protection. Thus, mangroves can help shield coastlines from storm-driven water, especially when the forests are broad and intact.
questions.question: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.A: Broad, healthy mangrove forests can reduce the force of storm-driven water along coastlines.
choices.B: The red mangrove is the most common plant found throughout Florida’s Everglades.
choices.C: Researchers have found that storms are becoming more frequent in the Ten Thousand Islands.
choices.D: Mangrove roots are more important to coastal ecosystems than mangrove trunks are.

questions.explanation: The passage explains that mangroves can reduce the energy of storm-driven water and that broader, intact forests provide greater protection. The other choices focus on details that are either unsupported or not central to the passage.

questions.passage: Along Florida’s Ten Thousand Islands, stands of red mangrove (*Rhizophora mangle*) differ considerably in width and condition. Measurements of water moving through these forests indicate that the tangled trunks and aerial roots dissipate some of the energy carried by storm-driven water. The effect is not uniform, however: water passing through a narrow stand encounters fewer obstacles, while damaged vegetation likewise provides less resistance. These observations suggest that simply having mangroves along a shoreline does not guarantee the same degree of protection everywhere. Rather, the capacity of a mangrove forest to moderate storm impacts depends in part on how continuous and extensive the forest is.
questions.question: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.A: Red mangroves are especially well adapted to the environmental conditions of Florida’s Ten Thousand Islands.
choices.B: Mangrove forests can moderate storm-driven water, but the degree of protection depends partly on the forests’ extent and condition.
choices.C: Narrow mangrove stands are generally more vulnerable to storm damage than wide mangrove stands.
choices.D: The aerial roots of red mangroves dissipate more storm energy than their trunks do.

questions.explanation: The passage connects two ideas: mangrove vegetation dissipates some of the energy carried by storm-driven water, but the effect varies with the forest’s width and condition. Choice B combines both ideas into the central conclusion. A and D focus on narrower details, while C introduces a claim about vulnerability to damage that the passage does not establish.

questions.passage: In Florida’s Ten Thousand Islands, red mangroves create physical resistance to storm-driven water through their trunks and aerial roots. Measurements across stands of different widths showed that water lost energy while moving through the vegetation, making mangrove cover appear useful as a coastal buffer. The measurements also revealed an important complication: two shorelines could contain the same species while differing greatly in the amount of vegetation intercepting incoming water. Narrow stands presented fewer obstacles, and gaps caused by vegetation loss likewise reduced resistance. In a comparison of two shorelines with similar mangrove species, the broader and more continuous stand reduced water velocity more consistently across the protected area. The contrast meant that researchers could not treat the mere presence of mangroves as a sufficient measure of their protective effect.
questions.question: Which choice best states the central idea of the text?

choices.A: The protective value of red mangroves is determined primarily by the number of aerial roots in a coastal forest.
choices.B: Measurements from the Ten Thousand Islands demonstrate that storm-driven water causes extensive damage whenever mangrove forests are narrow.
choices.C: Red mangrove forests can lessen the energy of storm-driven water, although the amount of protection depends partly on the extent and continuity of the vegetation.
choices.D: The presence of red mangroves along a shoreline is insufficient to prevent storms from carrying water inland.

questions.explanation: The passage first establishes that mangrove vegetation can reduce the energy of moving water, then shows that the effect varies with how much and how continuously the vegetation intercepts that water. Choice C captures both the benefit and the qualification. A focuses on one feature, B overstates the evidence, and D turns a qualification about degree of protection into an absolute claim.

questions.passage: In ancient Pompeii, electoral messages called *programmata* were painted on walls along busy streets such as the Via dell'Abbondanza. These messages supported candidates for local office and sometimes named individual people or groups that endorsed them. Because political recommendations appeared in ordinary public spaces rather than only in official buildings, they provide evidence that political advocacy in Pompeii involved people outside the city's formal officeholders.
questions.question: What can reasonably be inferred from the passage about political advocacy in Pompeii?

choices.A: Most Pompeians supported the candidates named in public inscriptions.
choices.B: Political candidates were usually selected by wealthy patrons.
choices.C: Political advocacy in Pompeii was not limited to formal city officials.
choices.D: The Via dell'Abbondanza served as Pompeii's main political institution.

questions.explanation: The passage points out that electoral messages appeared in ordinary public spaces and sometimes identified people or groups endorsing candidates. These details support the inference that political advocacy extended beyond formal officeholders. The other choices make claims about the majority of Pompeians, candidate selection, or the importance of the street that the passage does not establish.

questions.passage: At Pompeii, electoral *programmata* appeared on walls along routes such as the Via dell'Abbondanza, where pedestrians could encounter recommendations for candidates seeking local office. Some inscriptions identify individual endorsers, while others refer to occupational or neighborhood groups. These messages cannot show how many Pompeians actually voted or how influential any particular endorsement was. They do show, however, that political advocacy was displayed in ordinary public spaces and could involve people and groups beyond those who held political office. The evidence therefore suggests that civic advocacy was connected to social relationships outside Pompeii's formal political institutions.
questions.question: Which inference is best supported by the passage?

choices.A: Political advocacy in Pompeii could extend through social networks beyond formal officeholders.
choices.B: Most occupational groups in Pompeii officially endorsed political candidates.
choices.C: The *programmata* were more influential than Pompeii's elections themselves.
choices.D: Neighborhood groups usually selected candidates for local office.

questions.explanation: The passage describes endorsements by individuals and groups and emphasizes that these messages appeared in ordinary public spaces. Although the inscriptions cannot establish the number of voters or the influence of particular endorsements, they support the inference that political advocacy extended through social relationships beyond formal officeholders. B, C, and D go beyond the evidence.

questions.passage: Pompeii's electoral inscriptions complicate the idea that local politics was conducted mainly within formal political spaces. Along streets such as the Via dell'Abbondanza, *programmata* recommended candidates for local office and sometimes identified individual endorsers or occupational and neighborhood groups. Their placement meant that political advocacy formed part of the visual environment encountered in everyday urban life. Yet the inscriptions reveal less about the scale of participation than about the existence of advocacy: they cannot establish how many people supported a candidate, whether an endorsement persuaded voters, or how many endorsers actually participated in an election. Even so, the range of people and groups represented in these messages suggests that political expression was connected to social relationships extending beyond officeholders themselves. The evidence therefore points to a political culture in which formal institutions existed alongside broader forms of publicly expressed civic advocacy, although the precise extent of that involvement remains uncertain.
questions.question: Which inference about Pompeii's political life is best supported by the passage?

choices.A: Because *programmata* were publicly visible, most Pompeians probably voted for the candidates they endorsed.
choices.B: Occupational and neighborhood groups held more political power than Pompeii's formal officeholders.
choices.C: The *programmata* demonstrate that Pompeii's elections were primarily controlled by ordinary pedestrians.
choices.D: Political advocacy in Pompeii likely extended through everyday social relationships, even though the scale of participation cannot be determined from the inscriptions.

questions.explanation: The passage distinguishes between what the inscriptions demonstrate and what they cannot demonstrate. The variety of endorsers and the public placement of the *programmata* support the inference that political advocacy extended through everyday social relationships. However, the inscriptions do not reveal how many people actually participated or how influential the endorsements were. A, B, and C turn evidence of public advocacy into unsupported claims about majority behavior or political control.

questions.passage: At Pompeii, archaeologists have used ground-penetrating radar (GPR) to detect buried walls and other features beneath the site's surface. The scans can reveal patterns that may indicate structures that are difficult to see from above. Because researchers can survey an area before disturbing the ground, they can use the results to identify locations that deserve closer physical investigation. Thus, GPR can help archaeologists focus excavation on potentially informative areas.
questions.question: Which choice best supports the conclusion that GPR can help archaeologists use excavation more efficiently?

choices.A: GPR can reveal possible buried structures before archaeologists physically investigate the area.
choices.B: Pompeii contains structures from several periods of the city's history.
choices.C: Some buried features at Pompeii are difficult to detect from the surface.
choices.D: Archaeologists use several technologies when studying Pompeii.

questions.explanation: Choice A provides the direct link between GPR and more targeted excavation: researchers can identify possible structures before physically investigating them. The other choices provide relevant background but do not explain how GPR could make excavation more focused.

questions.passage: At Pompeii's House of Obellius Firmus, a georadar survey revealed several subsurface anomalies associated with buried wall structures. The results did not identify every feature with certainty; archaeological interpretation remained preliminary, and some locations required additional excavation to determine what the signals represented. Even so, the survey helped researchers distinguish areas containing potentially significant structural remains from portions of the site where fewer such anomalies were detected. Physical excavation could then be concentrated in places where the geophysical evidence suggested that further investigation might be especially informative. The radar therefore functioned less as a substitute for excavation than as a means of helping archaeologists decide where excavation could be most productive.
questions.question: Which choice best supports the conclusion that georadar helped archaeologists concentrate their excavation efforts?

choices.A: The survey revealed anomalies associated with buried wall structures, although their interpretation remained preliminary.
choices.B: Researchers used differences in the survey results to distinguish locations that warranted additional physical investigation.
choices.C: The House of Obellius Firmus contains buried structures that are not visible from the ground surface.
choices.D: Some features identified by the survey could not be interpreted with certainty without excavation.

questions.explanation: The conclusion concerns how georadar helped researchers concentrate excavation. Choice B connects the survey results to the researchers' decision about where to conduct additional physical investigation. A and D describe limitations of the survey, while C merely describes the archaeological setting.

questions.passage: At Pompeii's House of Obellius Firmus, archaeologists used georadar to investigate buried phases of the building. The survey produced subsurface anomalies consistent with wall structures, but the signals did not reveal the complete form or history of those structures. Some interpretations remained tentative because different subsurface conditions could produce similar patterns. Excavation of selected areas then provided physical remains that could be compared with the radar interpretations. Where the two kinds of evidence corresponded, archaeologists had stronger grounds for treating particular anomalies as meaningful architectural features; where they did not, excavation revealed questions that the radar data alone could not resolve. In several locations, the areas flagged by the survey became the places selected for closer physical investigation, while other signals were set aside for later study.
questions.question: Which choice best explains how the evidence in the passage supports the author's conclusion about the role of georadar?

choices.A: Because georadar sometimes produces uncertain signals, excavation remains the more reliable method for reconstructing Pompeii's buried architecture.
choices.B: Because the survey identified anomalies that were later compared with physical remains, georadar can contribute useful preliminary evidence even when it cannot independently resolve every archaeological question.
choices.C: Because some radar anomalies corresponded to buried walls, georadar can determine the construction history of the House of Obellius Firmus before excavation begins.
choices.D: Because excavation can confirm or complicate radar interpretations, archaeologists should postpone georadar surveys until after physical remains have been uncovered.

questions.explanation: The survey did not answer every archaeological question on its own, but its anomalies helped identify areas for later investigation and some were supported by physical remains. Choice B reflects both that usefulness and the limitation. A overstates the weakness of the method, C gives it more power than the passage supports, and D reverses the sequence described.

questions.passage: At the Red Mesa Research Station, engineers compared three photovoltaic arrays with the same rated capacity. The arrays received different amounts of sunlight and operated at different temperatures. Mesa received the most sunlight, at 7.4 hours per day, and produced the most electricity, at 20.1 kWh per day. However, Mesa also had the lowest efficiency, at 17.8%, while the cooler Juniper and Arroyo arrays had efficiencies of 19.2% and 19.5%, respectively.
questions.question: Which conclusion is best supported by the passage and table?

choices.A: Arroyo produced the most electricity because it had the highest efficiency.
choices.B: Higher temperatures caused all three arrays to produce more electricity.
choices.C: Mesa produced the most electricity even though it had the lowest efficiency.
choices.D: The three arrays received nearly identical amounts of sunlight.

questions.explanation: The table shows that Mesa had the highest daily electricity output but the lowest efficiency. The other choices contradict the data or make claims that the table does not establish.

questions.passage: At the Red Mesa Research Station, engineers compared three photovoltaic arrays with the same rated capacity to examine how different operating conditions related to performance. Mesa received substantially more sunlight than Juniper or Arroyo and consequently had the highest daily electricity output. Yet Mesa also operated at the highest average temperature and had the lowest efficiency. The efficiency figures therefore cannot be interpreted simply by looking at total electricity production: an array may generate more electricity while converting a smaller percentage of the available sunlight. The data consequently distinguish between the amount of electricity an array produces and the proportion of incoming sunlight that it converts.
questions.question: Which choice provides the best evidence for the passage's distinction between total electricity production and conversion efficiency?

choices.A: Mesa operated at the highest average temperature.
choices.B: Mesa produced the most electricity while having the lowest efficiency of the three arrays.
choices.C: Juniper and Arroyo had lower daily electricity outputs than Mesa.
choices.D: All three arrays had the same rated capacity.

questions.explanation: B combines the two pieces of evidence needed for the distinction: Mesa led in total electricity output but had the lowest efficiency. The other choices provide only one part of the comparison or establish a condition under which the comparison was made.

questions.passage: At the Red Mesa Research Station, engineers compared three photovoltaic arrays with the same rated capacity but different operating conditions. Mesa received 7.4 hours of sunlight per day, more than Juniper or Arroyo, and its 20.1 kWh daily output was the highest. Yet Mesa also had the lowest efficiency, 17.8%, compared with 19.2% for Juniper and 19.5% for Arroyo. The cooler arrays therefore converted a larger share of their available sunlight even though neither produced as much electricity overall. The data do not establish that temperature alone caused the efficiency difference, since the arrays operated under different conditions. The engineers also noted that Mesa's extra sunlight coincided with its higher output, while the efficiency figures moved in the opposite direction. These comparisons required the researchers to treat output and efficiency as separate measurements when evaluating the arrays.
questions.question: Which statement best synthesizes the information in the passage and table?

choices.A: Mesa's lower efficiency shows that increasing the amount of available sunlight does not substantially affect total electricity production.
choices.B: Because Juniper and Arroyo converted more sunlight efficiently, they should be considered superior to Mesa by every meaningful measure.
choices.C: Mesa's output advantage and efficiency disadvantage show that total electricity production and conversion efficiency measure different aspects of photovoltaic performance.
choices.D: The higher operating temperature at Mesa definitively caused its lower efficiency despite its greater exposure to sunlight.

questions.explanation: Mesa leads in daily electricity output but has the lowest efficiency, so those measurements cannot be treated as interchangeable. The passage also warns that the data do not prove temperature alone caused the efficiency difference. Choice C captures the contrast without adding a claim the table does not establish.

questions.passage: At the University of Arizona Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research, scientists study the annual growth rings of ponderosa pines in northern Arizona. In years with more rainfall, these trees often form wider rings. Because rainfall from centuries ago was not measured directly, researchers can use tree-ring width as a **proxy** for past precipitation. Thus, the rings provide an indirect way to estimate how wet earlier periods were.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“proxy”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: A feature that changes independently of environmental conditions
choices.B: A record that reveals exactly how much rain fell
choices.C: A method for predicting where trees will grow
choices.D: A substitute measure used to estimate something indirectly

questions.explanation: The passage explains that past rainfall was not measured directly, so researchers use tree-ring width to estimate it. Therefore, proxy refers to a substitute measure that provides indirect information about something else.

questions.passage: Researchers at the University of Arizona Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research have used ponderosa pine chronologies from northern Arizona to reconstruct rainfall patterns from periods before weather instruments were available. Wider rings often occur during wetter years, so ring width can serve as a **proxy** for precipitation. The relationship is not exact, however, because temperature, soil conditions, and other environmental factors can also affect growth. Researchers therefore compare many trees and calibrate their ring patterns against periods for which instrumental rainfall measurements are available. Once those influences are taken into account, variations in tree growth can provide evidence about rainfall that was never directly recorded.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“proxy”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: A collection of measurements used to distinguish one tree from another
choices.B: An indirect indicator used to estimate a quantity that was not directly observed
choices.C: A complete record that can replace instrumental measurements
choices.D: A biological characteristic that remains unchanged under different environmental conditions

questions.explanation: The passage explains that researchers use ring patterns to infer past rainfall even though the rainfall itself was not directly measured. Because the relationship must be calibrated and other influences considered, proxy means an indirect indicator, not an exact record.

questions.passage: At the University of Arizona Laboratory of Tree-Ring Research, scientists use ponderosa pine chronologies from northern Arizona to study climate conditions that existed before systematic weather measurements. A wide ring may coincide with a wetter year, but the same ring can also reflect temperature, soil moisture, competition, or other influences. Researchers therefore compare patterns across many trees and test them against periods for which instrumental observations exist. When a relationship remains consistent across those comparisons, the older ring patterns can be interpreted with greater confidence. The method is especially useful for periods when no rain gauge or other instrument was operating. For each reconstruction, the researchers evaluate how well the calibrated ring pattern tracks the measured precipitation before applying the same relationship to earlier portions of the chronology; the resulting **proxy** is then used alongside other evidence about past conditions.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“proxy”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: A measurement that becomes unreliable whenever more than one environmental factor affects it
choices.B: A direct record preserved from the period being studied
choices.C: A measurement used in place of a directly observed variable after a reliable relationship between the two has been established
choices.D: A preliminary observation that must be discarded once instrumental records become available

questions.explanation: The passage shows that ring patterns are compared with periods of measured precipitation before they are used to interpret earlier periods. Thus, the target word refers to a measurement used as a stand-in for a variable that was not directly observed. A, B, and D conflict with the way the researchers validate and use the ring patterns.

questions.passage: Archaeologists studying pottery at the ancient settlement of Tel Haran first thought that the large number of painted bowls found there showed that the bowls had been made locally. However, chemical tests later showed that the clay came from a distant region, suggesting that many bowls had been imported. The researchers therefore described their first explanation as **provisional**, since the new evidence required them to reconsider it.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“provisional”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: Carefully documented
choices.B: Widely accepted
choices.C: Not yet final
choices.D: Based on chemical evidence

questions.explanation: The researchers had to reconsider their first explanation after receiving new evidence, so the explanation was provisional, or not yet final.

questions.passage: At Tel Haran, archaeologists initially connected the settlement's unusually large collection of painted bowls with local pottery production. The concentration seemed significant because nearby sites contained far fewer such vessels. Yet chemical analysis showed that the bowls' clay originated hundreds of kilometers away, making long-distance trade a plausible explanation. Some bowls also showed wear consistent with repeated use at Tel Haran, indicating that imported vessels could have accumulated there over time. For this reason, the researchers called their first explanation **provisional** rather than abandoning it entirely.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“provisional”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: Accepted as a reasonable possibility but still subject to reconsideration
choices.B: Supported primarily by evidence from nearby settlements
choices.C: Rejected because the pottery had been transported from elsewhere
choices.D: Established by the wear patterns found on the pottery

questions.explanation: The original explanation remained plausible, but the chemical and wear evidence prevented the researchers from treating it as settled. Thus, provisional means accepted for the time being but still open to reconsideration.

questions.passage: At Tel Haran, archaeologists initially connected the abundance of painted bowls with local production. The vessels were unusually common at the settlement, and fragments occurred in several areas where production debris might be expected. That interpretation remained **provisional**, however, because the distribution of fragments could also have resulted from repeated use of pottery obtained elsewhere. Chemical analysis later linked the clay to a distant region, strengthening the case for long-distance trade but not establishing that every vessel had arrived that way. Some bowls showed extensive wear consistent with prolonged use at Tel Haran, whereas others were relatively little worn. The differing wear patterns meant that the collection could reflect several stages of acquisition and use, so the researchers continued comparing pottery samples and trade evidence rather than treating the local-production explanation as settled.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“provisional”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: Formed from evidence that was sufficient to establish one explanation conclusively
choices.B: Treated as a working interpretation that remained open to change as new evidence emerged
choices.C: Developed mainly by comparing Tel Haran with other archaeological settlements
choices.D: Restricted to pottery whose clay could be traced to distant regions

questions.explanation: The original explanation is supported by some observations but challenged by the chemical and wear evidence, so the researchers continue testing it rather than treating it as settled. In context, **provisional** describes an interpretation that is being used for the time being but remains open to revision. The other choices either make the interpretation too certain or refer to details unrelated to the word's meaning.

questions.passage: Researchers at Eastview University tested tomato plants in two urban farms. Plants watered with a drip system produced more tomatoes than plants watered by hand. The researchers noted that the drip system delivered water slowly, reducing the amount lost to evaporation during hot afternoons. Because the plants received water more efficiently, their **yield** was higher.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“yield”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: Amount produced
choices.B: Amount watered
choices.C: Time required
choices.D: Temperature reached

questions.explanation: The passage compares how many tomatoes the plants produced, so yield refers to the amount produced.

questions.passage: At two urban farms, Eastview University researchers compared tomato plants watered by hand with plants using a drip system. The drip-watered plants produced more tomatoes, even though the researchers did not give them substantially more total water. This difference was especially noticeable on hot afternoons, when much of the water applied by hand evaporated before the plants could use it. Thus, the drip system's higher **yield** was associated with more effective delivery of water, although the researchers cautioned that the system did not increase the plants' total water supply.
questions.question: As used in the text, what does **“yield”** most nearly mean?

choices.A: Efficiency of water use
choices.B: Amount of tomatoes produced

Researchers examining restored oyster reefs along Maryland's Chesapeake Bay initially found that shorelines behind reefs often retained more sediment than nearby unprotected shorelines. Because the reefs also reduced incoming wave energy, wave attenuation appeared to be a straightforward explanation. Measurements complicated that interpretation: where currents carried sediment along the shoreline, a reef sometimes caused sediment to accumulate on one side while leaving another section more exposed. Later comparisons showed that reefs facing the dominant wave approach produced more consistent reductions in shoreline loss.

A subsequent Chesapeake Bay project showed a similar pattern but introduced another complication. Instruments recorded weaker waves behind several reefs, and those areas generally lost less sediment. At one site, however, a reef reduced wave energy while erosion increased farther along the adjacent shoreline because the structure altered a local current. Other reefs, positioned differently relative to prevailing waves and shoreline currents, produced more stable shoreline conditions.

questions.explanation: Text 1 shows that wave reduction can accompany lower sediment loss but that shoreline currents can redistribute sediment, while Text 2 supplies a case in which wave reduction occurred alongside increased erosion farther away.
